title: Our imputation means satisfaction’s effect—not denial of inherent justice
source_text: XXXVI. Jam vero quis nostrum aliud cogitavit, quum nos per solam Christi justitiam nobis imputatam justificari dixit, quam hoc ipsum Christum Deo Patri pro nobis satisfecisse, & eam satisfactionem ita nobis a Deo donari, & communicari, quum nos justificat, ut nostra satisfactio & justitia dici possit: adeoque remissionem culpae & sempiternae poenae, quam in justificatione nostra a Deo consequimur, esse effectum solius satisfactionis Christi, non vero justitiae ullius nobis inhaerentis? Aut quis inde collegit in nobis non esse justitiam per gratiam Christi productam, a qua vere justi nominemur & simus: quaeque vera sit atque absoluta, quoad essentiam, & partes integrantes, licet in gradibus a summa perfectione deficiat, eique multi naevi & maculae adhaereant ex quotidianis fidelium lapsibus: quod fatentur Doctores Ecclesiae Romanae, & nominatim Bellarminus ipse, ut in Thesibus de Justitia per Christi gratiam fidelibus inhaerente antea fuit a nobis probatum? Unde patet Scholae Romanae Theologos immerito carpere nostram de imputatione justitiae Christi doctrinam, quandoquidem nihil hac in parte revera sentimus, quod vis veritatis ipsos non cogat agnoscere.
pass_a_gloss: Now who among us thought anything else, when he said we are justified by Christ’s righteousness alone imputed to us, than this very thing: that Christ satisfied God the Father for us, and that that satisfaction is so given and communicated to us by God when he justifies us that it can be called our satisfaction and righteousness—and thus that the remission of fault and everlasting penalty which we obtain from God in our justification is an effect of Christ’s satisfaction alone, not of any righteousness inhering in us? Or who thence gathered that there is not in us a righteousness produced by Christ’s grace, by which we are truly named and are just—and which is true and absolute as to essence and integral parts, though it falls short in degrees from highest perfection and many flaws and stains cling to it from the faithful’s daily lapses—which the doctors of the Roman Church confess, and Bellarmine by name, as was previously proved by us in the Theses on Righteousness inhering in the faithful by Christ’s grace? Hence it is plain that the Roman school’s theologians unjustly carp at our doctrine of the imputation of Christ’s righteousness, since in this part we in truth think nothing that the force of truth does not compel them to acknowledge.
pass_b_english: Imputation language means: donated satisfaction is ours; remission is its alone effect—not inherent justice’s merit.
We still confess real though imperfect inherent holiness; Rome’s attack is undeserved.
